title: GreenCell Mobility raises ₹330 crore to add 4,500 electric buses
excerpt: Impact Fund Denmark invests ₹330 crore in NueGo operator GreenCell Mobility to roll out 4,500 e-buses and pass 5,000 buses across 105 Indian cities.
content:
GreenCell Mobility, which runs electric buses for state transport bodies and under its own NueGo brand, has raised ₹330 crore (about $34.6 million) in equity from Impact Fund Denmark, according to Inc42, which reported the deal on 12 October 2026. The money backs the rollout of roughly 4,500 e-buses already in its pipeline, which would take the fleet past 5,000 buses across 105 Indian cities.

The company did not disclose a valuation or the size of the stake Impact Fund Denmark bought.

Key takeaways

  • Impact Fund Denmark (IFDK) invested ₹330 crore in GreenCell Mobility as equity, not debt. A crore is 10 million rupees.
  • The capital supports about 4,500 e-buses in GreenCell's order book, which would lift its fleet above 5,000 buses in 105 cities.
  • GreenCell says it already runs more than 1,200 e-buses and over 270 charging stations, according to Inc42.
  • The round comes nine months after an $89 million mezzanine raise from IFC, British International Investment and Tata Capital.

The deal: who invested and why

Impact Fund Denmark is a Danish investor, and this is a direct equity bet on an Indian operator. Its chief executive Lars Bo Bertram called India a key market for the fund and pointed to electric transport as a way to tackle air pollution, according to Autoguideindia.

GreenCell is a portfolio company of Eversource Capital, a joint venture of Everstone Capital and Lightsource, as Inc42 reported. Its other existing backers include the International Finance Corporation (IFC, the World Bank's private-sector arm), British International Investment (BII, the UK's development finance institution) and Tata Capital, according to Entrepreneur India.

Managing director and CEO Devndra Chawla said the equity "gives us greater headroom to accelerate our plans", and that the focus stays on executing the order book and on reliable service, as Entrepreneur India reported. Dhanpal Jhaveri, CEO of Eversource Capital, framed the deal as a sign that investors now see electric public transport in India as investable infrastructure.

What GreenCell Mobility does

GreenCell was founded in 2019 and is based in Mumbai, according to Inc42. It does not make buses. It buys them from manufacturers under contract, then operates and maintains them, which is why it describes itself as OEM-agnostic, meaning it is not tied to one bus maker. Its model is often called electric mobility-as-a-service.

The business has two sides:

  • City buses for governments. Most of its fleet runs on intra-city routes for state and city transport undertakings. Inc42 counts about 900 intra-city buses, plus 50 for the Maharashtra State Road Transport Corporation (MSRTC).
  • NueGo intercity coaches. About 300 buses run intercity routes under its consumer brand NueGo, where passengers book tickets directly.

It also builds and runs charging infrastructure, with more than 270 charging stations, per the same report.

How GreenCell has funded itself so far

Electric bus operators need large sums up front, because they pay for the buses and chargers and recover the cost over contracts that can run a decade or more. GreenCell has leaned heavily on debt and development finance:

  • 2022: $55 million from the Asian Development Bank, the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank and the Clean Technology Fund, through its unit GreenCell Express, according to Inc42.
  • July 2023: ₹3,000 crore of debt from state-owned lender REC to acquire 3,000 e-buses and build charging, per the same report.
  • May 2024: a ₹307 crore project finance facility from Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corporation for 350 nine-metre air-conditioned e-buses in eight Uttar Pradesh cities.
  • January 2026: $89 million in mezzanine funding (a mix of debt and equity features) led by IFC, BII and Tata Capital, with a target of 3,700 vehicles at the time, according to Energetica India.

On financials, the most recent figures we could tie to a named outlet are old. Inc42, citing data from Tofler, reported revenue of ₹328.21 crore in FY23, up from ₹86.43 crore in FY22, while net profit fell to ₹0.71 crore from ₹11.92 crore. We did not find later audited numbers in reputable coverage, so we have left them out.

The government schemes behind the order book

GreenCell's growth rides on public money for electric buses. Three central schemes matter most.

PM-eBus Sewa

Approved by the Cabinet on 16 August 2023, PM-eBus Sewa aims to add 10,000 e-buses to city services on a public-private partnership model, at an estimated cost of ₹57,613 crore, of which the Centre provides ₹20,000 crore, according to the Press Information Bureau. It supports bus operations for 10 years across 169 cities, and states or cities run the services and pay the operators.

PM E-DRIVE

The PM E-DRIVE scheme, approved on 11 September 2024 with an outlay of ₹10,900 crore over two years, sets aside ₹4,391 crore for 14,028 e-buses for state transport undertakings, according to the Press Information Bureau. Convergence Energy Services Ltd (CESL) aggregates demand in nine large cities, including Delhi, Mumbai, Bengaluru and Hyderabad, and the scheme also funds 1,800 fast chargers for e-buses.

The payment security mechanism

Most of these buses are run on a gross cost contract (GCC): the operator buys and runs the bus, and the transport authority pays a fee per kilometre instead of paying for the bus up front. Operators have worried about late payments, so the Cabinet approved a ₹3,435.33 crore PM-eBus Sewa Payment Security Mechanism on 11 September 2024. CESL pays operators if an authority defaults, covering more than 38,000 e-buses from FY25 to FY29, according to the Press Information Bureau.

Rollout has been slow. As of 10 July 2026, that mechanism covered 27,555 e-buses, but only 523 had been deployed under it, the Ministry of Heavy Industries told Parliament, per a PIB release dated 4 August 2026.

Why it matters

The gap between buses sanctioned and buses on the road is where operators like GreenCell earn their place. Winning tenders is one step; financing, delivering and running thousands of buses is harder, and it needs patient equity alongside cheap debt. Fresh equity also gives GreenCell a larger base to raise more debt against.

The investment also fits a wider pattern. Inc42 noted that investors are now backing the operating platforms in India's e-bus business, not just the assets, pointing to KKR's commitment of up to $310 million in PMI Electro Mobility's platform. For GreenCell, the next 18 to 24 months will show whether it can convert a 4,500-bus pipeline into reliable service. Follow more rounds on our funding tracker and in startup news.

FAQ

How much did GreenCell Mobility raise?

₹330 crore, about $34.6 million, in equity from Impact Fund Denmark, reported on 13 October 2026.

Who owns GreenCell Mobility?

It is a portfolio company of Eversource Capital. IFC, British International Investment, Tata Capital and now Impact Fund Denmark are also investors. Shareholding percentages have not been published.

Is NueGo part of GreenCell?

Yes. NueGo is GreenCell's intercity electric coach brand, with about 300 buses, according to Inc42.

What is a gross cost contract?

A model where a private operator buys, runs and maintains buses for a transport authority, which pays a fixed fee per kilometre rather than buying the buses itself.

What is the PM E-DRIVE scheme?

A ₹10,900 crore central scheme approved in September 2024 to support electric two-wheelers, three-wheelers, trucks, ambulances, chargers and 14,028 e-buses.
